title: The bardo
hookLine: teachings on the in-between after death; a text read aloud to the dying

lines: A SONG, A PSALM, A LETTER.
HEARING, AMONG THE LAST TO FADE.
A TEXT READ ALOUD BESIDE THE DYING.
cards: A favorite song. A psalm. A letter from a grandchild.
In hospice rooms, near the end, families sometimes read or play something to the one who is dying. Hospice staff are taught that hearing may be among the last senses to fade.

Tibetan Buddhists have a whole text for that moment, read aloud beside the dying, and then beside the body for days afterward. It speaks directly to the one who has died, in a calm voice, telling them where they are.

teach.b: Bardo is Tibetan for the in-between, a gap between one state and the next.

Tibetan teachers describe several: the in-between of this life, of dreams, of meditation, of dying, and then, after death, the stages before a new birth. They teach that this last passage can last up to forty-nine days.
First, they say, comes a moment of clear light, like a cloudless sky. If it isn't recognized, visions arise, peaceful and then fierce, and finally the mind is drawn toward a new life.

The text that guides this is called, in Tibetan, Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between. Tradition says Padmasambhava composed it and hid it, and that a treasure-finder named Karma Lingpa found it centuries later.
In the West it's known as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a title given by its first English editor.

A lama or friend reads it near the one who has died, and its message, over and over, is simple: don't be afraid; these appearances are your own mind; recognize them, and be free. Buddhist traditions differ here.
The Theravada Abhidhamma teaches that rebirth follows immediately, without an in-between, though some Theravada teachers allow for one.
The Tibetan schools, and some other Mahayana traditions, teach the in-between in detail, and East Asian Buddhist rites also mark forty-nine days after a death.

teach.h: EVERY MOMENT A KIND OF BARDO.
teach.b: And Tibetan teachers add one more thing: every moment is a kind of bardo.
Between jobs, between homes, between one breath and the next, things loosen, and change becomes possible. In between.

how: In Tibetan communities a lama or trained friend often reads the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and, after death, beside the body, and families hold rituals during the forty-nine days that follow; many Theravada communities hold merit-making ceremonies for the dead instead.

o: the in-between state, as after death
a meditation posture for long retreats
a heaven where good souls rest forever

games.q: match the pieces of the bardo teaching.
p: don't be afraid; recognize your mind

games.q: someone you know has died, and their Tibetan family asks a lama to come. what does the lama most likely do?
o: read a text aloud beside the body, speaking to the one who died.
read the person's life story to the family.
games.why: the Bardo Thödol is read to the one who has died: don't be afraid, these appearances are your own mind, recognize them.

practice: This one asks for a gentle heart, so go easy: if you're willing, let one thing come that you'd want read to you at the very end, a verse, a song, a few words from someone you love, without deciding anything.
Then let it go, and rest in the small gap at the end of each out-breath, the tiny in-between before the next breath comes.

wordCard.voice: Bardo. The in-between: in Tibetan teaching, the passage between death and rebirth, and every gap where change becomes possible.
